title: A Café Where Nothing Is Sold
text:
On the first Friday of every month, the community center in Bellview becomes a repair café. Despite its name, it does not sell coffee or repair services. Residents bring broken lamps, toys, bicycles, and small household objects. Volunteers sit beside them and show them how to examine and repair each item.

The organizers began the café after noticing how many useful objects were being thrown away. They hoped to reduce waste, but another benefit soon appeared. People who had never met began sharing tools and advice. A retired electrician now teaches teenagers how to replace damaged wires safely, while a university student helps older residents fix simple computer problems.

Not every object can be saved. If a repair would be dangerous or cost more than a replacement, volunteers explain this clearly. Even then, visitors often say the trip was worthwhile because they learned why the object failed. During its first year, the café examined 640 items and repaired almost three quarters of them. The organizers now plan to publish short repair guides based on the problems they see most often.

questions.question: Which service is NOT offered at the repair café?
What additional benefit appeared after the café began?
options: Useful objects were discarded more quickly

questions.question: What does the text say about the 640 items examined in the first year?
options: Fewer than one quarter could be repaired

questions.question: What is the main idea of the text?
options: A community project helps people repair objects and share skills
A café has found a new way to sell electrical tools
Teenagers are better at repairs than older residents
Most broken objects are too dangerous to repair

title: Starting Forty Minutes Later
text:
North Valley School tested a later starting time for one term. Classes normally began at 7:45, but during the test they began at 8:25. The school did not shorten the day. It reduced the long morning break and moved two weekly activities to the afternoon.

Before the change, students completed a survey about sleep and concentration. Teachers also recorded late arrivals and unfinished first-period assignments. The same information was collected at the end of the term. Late arrivals fell by 28 percent, and more students said they felt alert during the first lesson. However, the number of unfinished assignments changed very little.

The later start also created difficulties. Some parents began work early and could not drive their children at the new time. Sports teams had less daylight for outdoor practice in winter. The principal therefore warned against describing the test as a complete success. She said the results were encouraging, but the school would need new transport and sports arrangements before making the change permanent. The school board will review these practical issues before voting in June.

questions.question: What happened to the length of the school day during the test?
options: It was reduced by forty minutes

questions.question: Which result was connected with the later starting time?
What will happen before the school board votes in June?
options: The board will examine transport and sports problems
The school will cancel all afternoon activities
Teachers will stop recording late arrivals

questions.question: The pilot suggests that a later start may improve —
options: the length of the school day

title: Messages from an Old Hotel
text:
While renovating the Grand Lake Hotel, workers found a wooden box under a staircase. It contained more than two hundred postcards written by hotel guests between 1924 and 1951. Most cards had never been mailed. Some described family holidays, while others contained short notes that guests apparently planned to finish later.

The hotel owner gave the box to the town archive. Rather than displaying only the most beautiful cards, the archive created a searchable online collection. Volunteers typed every message and added information about the places and events mentioned. They did not publish home addresses or other private details.

The cards have already helped researchers understand how tourism changed in the area. Early visitors often arrived by train and stayed for several weeks. Later cards mention private cars and much shorter trips. Yet the collection is also valuable for ordinary families. One resident recognized her grandmother’s handwriting and discovered a description of a childhood picnic that no one in the family remembered. The archive is now asking residents to help identify people who appear in the postcard photographs.

questions.question: What did workers find under the hotel staircase?
options: A box containing more than two hundred old postcards
A collection of modern car advertisements
A list of every hotel employee
A finished book about local tourism

questions.question: The online collection is “searchable.” This means users can —
options: look for particular information in it
send the postcards to their owners

questions.question: In the final sentence, the word “people” refers to people —
options: who worked in the town archive

questions.question: What can researchers learn from the postcards?
options: How travel habits in the area changed over time
Why every guest forgot to mail a card
How the hotel was built under the staircase
Which modern cars are most popular

title: Mapping the Sounds of a City
text:
A group of college students has created a digital sound map of their city. Instead of showing streets and buildings, the map allows users to hear short recordings from different locations. These include the morning market, waves near the harbor, a basketball game, and bells from an old clock tower.

The students began the project because they believed that ordinary sounds are an important part of local history. A photograph can show what a place looked like, they explained, but it cannot record the voice of a street seller or the noise of a workshop. To make the collection useful, every recording includes its date, exact location, and a short description.

Residents may send in recordings, but the students review them before publication. They reject files that include private conversations or were recorded in unsafe places. They also ask contributors not to remove all background noise, since that noise often gives the recording its meaning. The team hopes future residents will use the map to compare the city’s sound environment with the way it sounds today.

questions.question: The words “These include” refer to examples of —
Why did the students create the sound map?
options: To preserve everyday sounds as part of local history
To replace every photograph in the city archive
To measure how loudly college students speak

questions.question: Why are contributors asked to keep some background noise?
options: It can help show what the place really sounded like
It makes private conversations easier to hear
It reduces the size of the digital file

questions.question: Which recording is most likely to be accepted?
options: A clear recording of harbor sounds with its date and location
An exciting file made in a dangerous area
A silent file from which all background sound was removed
